title: Three pillars (Avot 1:2)
hook: Simon the Just: the world stands on Torah, worship and deeds of kindness

segments.voice: Yesterday, metunim: the Great Assembly's call to be deliberate in judgment. Your line was judge slowly. Today, one of the last members of that Assembly gets his own saying. Day two hundred thirty-five.

Try sitting on a two-legged stool. You can do it, for a while, if you concentrate, feet planted. But the minute you relax, you tip. Add a third leg, and you can sit there all afternoon without thinking about it. Three is the smallest number that stands on its own. A lot of lives are two-legged stools. All work and worship, no kindness. All kindness, no learning. Leaning hard, one bad day from tipping over. An old sage named Simon had a saying about what the whole world rests on.
screen: `A TWO-LEGGED STOOL.` → `THREE STANDS ON ITS OWN.` → `WHAT THE WORLD RESTS ON.`

segments.voice: Simon the Just, Shimon HaTzaddik, was, tradition says, a high priest, and Avot says he was one of the last of the Great Assembly. His saying: on three things the world stands. On Torah. On avodah, worship. And on gemilut chasadim, deeds of loving-kindness. Torah is learning: studying, asking, understanding. Avodah, in Simon's day, meant the service in the Temple in Jerusalem, the offerings the priests brought there. Gemilut chasadim is kindness you do with your hands and time: visiting the sick, comforting mourners, lending without interest, helping a bride, burying the dead. Then the unthinkable happened. Rome destroyed the Temple. One of the three pillars fell. How does the world stand now? The rabbis gave two answers. First, avodah became prayer; the Talmud calls prayer the service of the heart. Second, an old story tells of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai walking past the ruins with his student, who cried: the place where our sins were atoned is destroyed. The teacher said, don't grieve, we have another way, just as good: deeds of loving-kindness. And he quoted the prophet Hosea, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." So the three legs are still there. Learning, prayer, kindness. And the stool only stands when all three touch the ground.
screen: `SIMON THE JUST, HIGH PRIEST.` · `TORAH, AVODAH, KINDNESS.` · `ROME DESTROYS THE TEMPLE.` · `I DESIRE MERCY, NOT SACRIFICE.` · then, large: `THREE LEGS TO STAND ON.`

segments.voice: Plan one of each for today. First, learning: one thing you'll read or ask about. Then a pause, for a prayer if you pray or a quiet minute if you don't, and one act of kindness: whose day can you make lighter with your hands or your time?
Three pillars. Simon the Just's saying in Avot: the world stands on Torah, on worship, and on deeds of loving-kindness.
Your line: three legs to stand on. Lose one, and the other two wobble. That's day two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Torah study, daily prayer and gemilut chasadim structure much of traditional Jewish life, and Simon the Just's saying is also sung, in Hebrew, as a song: al shloshah devarim.
